summary: Wilde reported to Robert Ross that Omero talked about him constantly, suspected him of treachery, and did not believe he would come back - and asked Ross what he had meant by a remark about Omero's conduct.
certainty_reasoning: SECOND-HAND: Wilde is the only witness, writing to one party about the other, and neither of them speaks here. WHAT CARRIES IT IS JEALOUSY. 'Treachery' from an absent man is unfaithfulness, not commercial betrayal; 'talks much - a little too much - of you' is Wilde being wry about someone who will not stop discussing an absent person; and 'your immediate return seems to him problematical' is a man who does not believe he is coming back. Taken together it is the shape of a lovers' quarrel relayed by a mutual friend, and jealousy is an expression of attachment. THIS EDGE WAS FIRST DECLINED and then drawn, 2026-08-06, per Lovelle. The original reasoning - that nothing here 'asserts attraction' - was inconsistent with the map's own practice: `boulton` is flagged as its batch's strongest attraction candidate on exactly this signal, Wilde's pique that a young man preferred someone else's company. WHAT COMPLICATES IT, recorded rather than smoothed: Ross handled Wilde's money and affairs, so 'treachery' could conceivably be practical, and 'revision' could be a manuscript. Neither reading explains 'talks much - a little too much - of you', which is about volume of feeling and not about business. NOTHING SEXUAL IS ESTABLISHED, no direction is asserted - the feeling on the page is Omero's, but nothing records what Ross felt - and no age is given for Omero.

sources.quote: Homer talks much - a little too much - of you. He slightly suspects you of treachery, and your immediate return seems to him problematical. Your allusion to his conduct on a postcard was mysterious. How was the 'revision' painful?
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [April 1900], Rome - the opening of the letter, quoted whole. 'Homer' is Omero anglicised, and it is only this English form that ties the two references to one person. Wilde is relaying one friend's grievances about another and asking Ross what he had meant by his own remark. The 'revision' is scare-quoted, unexplained on the page, and nothing is inferred about it here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Omero's jealousy of Ross, reported by Wilde to Ross himself.
